761: D is correct because a custom identity broker authenticates users against the on-premises LDAP directory and then calls AWS STS to obtain short-lived credentials, which is the required pattern when the identity provider does not support SAML federation. The broker validates the LDAP credentials and maps the user to an appropriate IAM role, limiting risk through temporary credentials. Federation-based options or rotating long-term IAM credentials do not work with a non-SAML directory.
762: C is correct because a retention rule in Recycle Bin automatically preserves deleted AMIs and their snapshots for a defined period so they can be recovered quickly and directly from the Recycle Bin. This is a native AWS feature designed specifically to recover accidentally deleted AMIs with no additional infrastructure, scheduling, or storage orchestration. Periodic AMI copies or separate EBS snapshots require custom automation and duplicate storage costs.
763: B is correct because ordering multiple AWS Snowball devices physically ships the 150 TB of data to AWS well within the one-month deadline, whereas the 100 Mbps night-only connection can only move a small fraction of that volume in the time available. Snowball is a managed, cost-effective offline transfer service for datasets that exceed network capacity. Any network-based approach such as Transfer Acceleration or a VPN would remain constrained by the same limited link and miss the deadline.
764: B is correct because keeping the web and application tiers on Amazon EC2 preserves the existing third-party VM architecture with the fewest possible changes, while Aurora MySQL is MySQL-compatible and supports point-in-time recovery through continuous incremental backups. Aurora also provides automated storage growth, self-healing storage, and high availability, reducing operational overhead. Placing the web tier in public subnets and the application and database tiers in private subnets follows standard three-tier security design.
765: C is correct because an SQS access policy is a resource-based policy attached directly to the queue, which can grant the other company's account permission to poll it without the vendor needing any permissions in the development team's account. The queue's own policy controls exactly which external principals may consume it. Identity-based IAM policies in the development team's account cannot be attached to identities in another account, and SNS or instance profile options do not provide queue-level cross-account access.
766: D is correct because AWS Systems Manager Session Manager provides secure shell access to EC2 instances in private subnets without opening inbound ports, managing SSH keys, or running bastion hosts, and the instances can reach the required SSM endpoints through the existing NAT gateway. Attaching the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the instances' IAM role is all that is needed for the developers, whether remote or in the office. This is the most cost-effective approach because it eliminates the ongoing cost of bastion hosts or additional VPN connections.
767: C is correct because a Storage Gateway volume gateway with cached volumes stores the primary data in Amazon S3 while keeping a frequently accessed subset on a local cache, giving researchers low-latency access to the working dataset they need immediately. Since the entire dataset is not accessed daily, moving the bulk of it to S3 eliminates the ongoing capital expense of expanding on-premises storage arrays. This cached volume model is purpose-built for exactly this access pattern.
768: A is correct because DynamoDB point-in-time recovery provides continuous backups that allow the table to be restored to any second within the last 35 days, easily covering the 24-hour requirement. It is a native, fully managed feature enabled with a single console setting, giving the least operational overhead. Hourly Lambda backups or capturing streams to S3 require custom code and management, and scheduled AWS Backup snapshots restore only to backup points rather than any point in time.
769: B is correct because S3 object-created event notifications can invoke a Lambda function directly, and Lambda is ideal for short sub-5-second metadata extraction while automatically scaling from a few files per hour to hundreds of concurrent uploads. This event-driven, pay-per-use architecture is highly cost-effective because compute is only consumed when a file actually arrives. Adding Kinesis Data Streams or SNS as intermediaries would introduce unnecessary infrastructure and cost for such simple per-file processing.
770: C is correct because Compute Savings Plans provide discounted pricing in exchange for a commitment and are ideal for the production instances' constant usage across time zones, while On-Demand billing matches the nonproduction instances that run only during business hours. Shutting down the nonproduction instances when not in use eliminates charges for idle capacity, especially on weekends. Reserved Instances, Dedicated Hosts, or EC2 Instance Savings Plans would commit to capacity that the intermittent nonproduction workload does not need.
771: C is correct because AWS SCT converts the Oracle schema to the Aurora PostgreSQL schema, and AWS DMS can perform a full load of the existing data plus ongoing change data capture replication, so every change made to the source database during the migration is captured and applied to the target. This SCT plus DMS combination is the standard AWS approach for heterogeneous database migrations with minimal downtime. A full-load-only task would miss changes that occur mid-migration, and DataSync or Snowball only move static data.
772: A is correct because Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate runs Docker containers as a fully managed serverless compute service, scaling in and out with demand on each service while requiring no EC2 infrastructure to provision or manage. B is correct because Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate provides the same benefit for Kubernetes workloads, running pods without managing worker nodes. Options using EC2 worker nodes add infrastructure to manage, and Lambda cannot run Docker containers as a hosting solution.
773: D is correct because an Auto Scaling group configured to scale out as traffic increases, using a launch template that starts new instances from a preconfigured AMI, provides automatic elasticity to handle the sudden spikes of the seasonal sale. This is the most cost-effective design because extra capacity is only paid for when the traffic actually arrives. Oversizing the group, keeping pre-stopped instances, or relying on pre-populated caches all waste money by paying for peak capacity continuously.
774: B is correct because the restricted-ssh AWS Config managed rule automatically and continuously evaluates every security group for rules allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 and flags violations the moment they are created. Pairing it with an Amazon SNS notification provides immediate alerting of any policy breach with almost no setup or ongoing administration. A custom Lambda monitoring script or an SCP approach would require development, ongoing maintenance, and would not detect breaches as directly.
775: B is correct because Amazon VPC Lattice provides managed service-to-service connectivity and discovery through a service network, letting microservices communicate over HTTPS listeners across accounts and VPCs with the least administrative overhead. Its built-in service registry handles service discovery, and targets can be Lambda functions or EKS-hosted compute registered directly. Network Firewall, PrivateLink with NLBs, or VPC peering all require significant per-connection configuration and lack an integrated service registry.
776: C is correct because Amazon ElastiCache for Redis serves frequently read metadata with sub-millisecond latency, offloading the read-heavy workload from the RDS instance since simply scaling the database will not help. Redis meets all stated requirements because it supports snapshots for persistence and replication for high availability. Memcached is the wrong cache choice here because it provides neither snapshots nor replication.
777: A is correct because adding the development OU's ARN to the launch permission list shares the AMIs with all accounts within that OU, which is the supported way to share AMIs across an organizational unit in AWS Organizations. C is correct because the AMIs are built from KMS-encrypted snapshots, so the key policy must additionally grant the development OU permission to use the KMS key for decryption; launch permissions alone are not sufficient for encrypted AMIs. Sharing to the Organizations root ARN would expose the AMIs to every account in the organization rather than only the development OU.
778: B is correct because ordering multiple AWS Snowball Edge storage-optimized devices allows the data at all 80 offices to be transferred in parallel and imported into Amazon S3, meeting the 4-week deadline despite the limited 1-2 Gbps office bandwidth. For a one-time migration, this avoids the large cost of provisioning 80 new 10 Gbps Direct Connect connections that would sit unused afterward. A single Snowmobile is designed for exabyte-scale data consolidated in one location, and Storage Gateway transfers would be throttled by each office's bandwidth.
779: B is correct because an EFS file system resource policy can explicitly deny the elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite action for the IAM roles attached to the EC2 instances, enforcing read-only access at the file system level using IAM access control as required. A resource-based deny cannot be overridden by the identities' other permissions, ensuring the applications can never modify or delete the dataset. Read-only mounts and POSIX permissions are not IAM-based controls and can be bypassed by privileged users.
780: A is correct because creating an IAM role in the company's account with a trust policy that lets the vendor's IAM role assume it is the standard, most secure cross-account access model, providing temporary credentials obtained through AWS STS. The vendor's automated tool can assume the role from its own account and receive only the temporary, scoped permissions defined by the attached IAM policies, avoiding long-term credentials entirely. IAM users with passwords or keys create long-lived secrets to manage and rotate, and IAM groups cannot contain identities from another AWS account.
